newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - NYMEX fails to take off despite volatility.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - NYMEX fails to take off despite volatility.

text.p: Oil prices and volatility on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) hit five-year highs in 1996, but that was not enough to lure many dealers to trade oil at the exchange, which bills itself as the world's largest commodities futures market.

It is, in fact, changes in the oil industry itself -- the way it manages inventory and the way it trades -- which discouraged greater participation in NYMEX oil trading this year, a trend which is expected by some dealers to continue in 1997 and beyond, according to industry observers.
"I think open interest is going to continue sideways because the factors that have gotten us to this point are now entrenched," said Gerald Samuels, managing director of ARB Oil.

Open interest, the amount of long and short positions at the end of each trading session, reached a record for the crude contract in April but dropped steeply to levels approximating the general trend of 1994 and 1995, where they have remained. There was a particularly sharp drop in December, even while volatility shot up again.

Cumulative crude trading volume to December 20 was up by about two percent to 23.3 million lots from 22.8 million in 1995. But that small increase came in a year when prices soared by more than 50 percent to new post-Gulf War highs and volatility reached 70 percent.
Oil products futures also had a slow year considering the price increase in both heating oil and gasoline.
Heating oil volatility was running at around 50 percent in the late spring and there was a spectacular 50 percent run-up in prices from June to October's post-Gulf War high.

Open interest had a spurt during the bull run but peaked in early October and has since slumped. For most of the year it has followed the declining trend of the last few years, though cumulative volume to December 20 was up about four percent at 8,169,517 lots.

Similarly, gasoline futures had an erratic but generally disappointing performance. Despite high price volatility, open interest was running below 1995's levels for most of the year and cumulative volume dropped to 6,204,214 from 6,855,737.

Participation in the gasoline contract has been depressed since 1994 when the NYMEX contract called for delivery of reformulated gasoline to conform to new U.S. Environmental Protection Agency regulations.
"Gasoline is so subject to political whims, and it has discouraged hedging with the (NYMEX) contract," said Samuels.

Some market players said that uncertainty about the on-off Iraq-United Nations "oil-for-food" deal, one of the main causes of price volatility this year, was actually a factor in discouraging market participation.
"Volatility is good, but not too much," said William Brown, president of trading firm W.H. Brown.
Also, the refining industry's move toward a "just-in-time" inventory management policy is reckoned to be a contributory factor in declining open interest in crude and heating oil.
Heating oil inventories hit record lows this year, leading to worries of a shortage and sending heating oil futures into steep "backwardation," where nearby prices are higher than forward prices.

The "backwardation" itself led to fewer refiners and heating oil retailers using the futures market as there was no price incentive to buy and store the product if it couldn't be sold at a later date in the futures market at a higher price.

"There has been a lack of participation by anyone who would have an interest in storing heat. This just-in-time management has decreased the ability to hedge," said Al Lindseth, manager of oil and gas hedge programs at GSC Energy.
"The inventory 'game' has actually decreased the need to hedge since they are now better managing supply," adds James Cordier of Allendale Inc.
Also, dealers said refiners are still leaning more toward the "over-the-counter" market, where Wall Street firms make markets in tailor-made contracts more specifically suited to refiner needs.
"It's the over-the-counter business with tailor-made deals for the customer which has taken away business from the Exchange," said Thomas Blakeslee, an analyst at Cargill Investor Services.
"I don't see the trend for these deals changing," said Warren Tashnek, president of Fimat USA Futures, adding "People like the convenience of being able to set your own margins."

NYMEX acknowledges increased competition from over-the-counter deals and the sideways movement in open interest. However, NYMEX president Patrick Thompson said business has instead been moving to NYMEX's options market.
"People like to reduce their risk on the upside and the downside, and try to make profits in between there," said Thompson in a telephone interview, explaining the growth in the options business.
"I don't think we have lost business . . . but we are seeing a change in the complexion of the market," said Thompson.
((-- New York Energy Desk, +1 212 859 1620))
